🎧 MiPAL Sends Sound in a Narrow Beam

Researchers at POSTECH built MiPAL, a parametric speaker with one emitter and 2 metamaterial layers. A front acoustic metasurface focuses ultrasound, while elastic metacells suppress vibrations that would spread audio sideways.

MiPAL modulates an ultrasonic wave with an audio signal, using nonlinear behavior in air to send sound along a narrow path. Tests in a mock aircraft cabin covered 500 Hz to 10 kHz, while the adjacent seat stayed quiet.

The modules are 3D-printed, so the design can be adapted to seat spacing, beam angle, or other conditions. Possible uses include personal announcements on planes and audio guides at museum displays.

📍 World Labs Unveils 3D Model Atlas

Atlas reconstructs a surrounding space in 3D from text or visual files. Users can then move the camera and change the view while the scene geometry stays intact.

With several photos, it builds a complete 3D space. From one image, it can infer hidden parts, while more source frames improve accuracy. Atlas also generates controllable video up to 1 minute in 1440p, with the camera path set directly. The same system can turn footage of a real room into a simulation for robot training.

Atlas is currently available only to early-access partners. It will later serve as the basis for new versions of Marble and other World Labs products.

And if those agents eventually become conscious, there could be vastly more simulated conscious beings than beings in the original “base” reality.

That’s essentially Nick Bostrom’s simulation argument except instead of being a distant philosophical thought experiment, AI is making the first steps toward it look increasingly tangible.

🍏 Jobs Letter Comes With Apple I

An Apple I linked to Fred Hatfield is going to auction on October 14. Bonhams estimates it at $500,000 to $800,000. The lot includes Steve Jobs’s 1978 reply to Hatfield, who had complained that Apple computers had no software.

Jobs offered to exchange Hatfield’s Apple I without memory, plus a $400 check, for an Apple II board with 4 KB. Hatfield declined. He later sold the machine for $40,000. In 2013, it fetched $671,400.

The computer still works. It is Apple I No. 48, with Steve Wozniak’s signature on the board. Only about 200 Apple Is were built, and fewer than 75 survive. Its original price was $666.66.

Researchers at Oak Ridge have developed an AI-based system capable of manipulating materials at the atomic level. This system autonomously arranges individual molecules and constructs custom structures atom by atom.

During a continuous 25-hour experiment, the AI assembled a synthetic graphene lattice made up of 37 molecules. The resulting structure displayed electronic properties as anticipated.

The long-term objective is to enable inverse material design: specifying desired properties and having the AI determine and create the necessary atomic arrangement.

🇯🇵 Japan is building AI satellites that could guide missiles

The country’s Defense Ministry is planning AI-equipped satellites capable of processing surveillance data directly in space, identifying potential enemy positions and predicting the movement of targets such as ships. These satellites won’t actually be doing the surveillance.

Instead, they’ll receive data collected by other satellites, analyze it onboard and send the processed targeting information directly to command centers on the ground.

That could dramatically reduce the time between detecting a target and acting on the information.

Japan is also exploring a system that could provide real-time targeting updates to long-range missiles after they’ve already been launched, potentially allowing them to adjust to moving targets and improve accuracy. 

Prototype development is planned for FY2027–2029, with space testing expected to begin from FY2030 onward.

❗️Three climbers trusted AI to plan their mountain trip and it went very wrong.

Three men set out to climb Mount Shasta in California after relying heavily on Google’s Gemini to help plan their route and decide what supplies to bring. They eventually had to be rescued. 

The group reached the summit at around 7 p.m. on August 30, roughly seven hours after the recommended noon turnaround time. They then started descending in darkness.

About an hour later, they became lost and contacted authorities for directions. Things got worse when they wandered into Mud Creek Canyon, where one of the climbers injured his knee.

The three were forced to spend the night stranded on the mountain before U.S. Forest Service climbing rangers reached them the following morning. They were given medical assistance and eventually escorted back to the trailhead.

Authorities later learned that AI had played a major role in their planning including advice on how much food and water to bring.

🧠 Researchers argue LLMs may never get us to AGI

21 researchers from Stanford, Oxford, DeepMind, CMU and Meta have published a paper called “Visual General Intelligence” and its argument is pretty brutal: Scaling LLMs might not be enough.

GPT-style models have shown that language can unlock impressive reasoning, but the researchers argue that text is ultimately a compressed description of reality. Words don’t directly teach a model how gravity works, how objects move, or how space behaves.

Humans learn many of these things before they can even speak. A baby doesn’t read about gravity. It experiences it.

The paper argues that future AI should be built around raw visual experience, images, spatial information and continuous video rather than treating vision as just another input for a language model.

By learning directly from the visual world, AI could develop stronger internal models of physics, cause and effect, objects and environments.

💰 The AI job bust just turned into a boom

Two years ago, AI was supposed to wipe out software jobs. Instead, developer hiring has bounced back above trend and developers are now the fastest-growing job category in the latest data from The Economist.

By 2026, AI-related white-collar work is around 700,000 jobs above where normal hiring would have put it.

And the boom isn’t limited to software. AI data centers are also creating roughly 300,000 extra jobs for electricians, plumbers and construction workers.

AI didn’t just replace jobs. It changed which skills companies are willing to pay for. The developers getting hired today are increasingly the ones who know how to work with AI, direct AI and build with AI.

And this pattern could spread far beyond coding. AI may replace some tasks, but people who know how to use it could become even more valuable.

⚡️An AI-designed drug may have made people biologically younger

Rentosertib just delivered a fascinating result: after 12 weeks of treatment, six different biological-age clocks all estimated patients to be roughly 3–4 years younger.

The six clocks came from independent groups, used different features and weren’t trained on the same data. Two measure mortality risk, while four track chronological age, yet they still moved in the same direction.

• 54 statistical tests. 21 were significant.
• By chance, only about 0.15 would be expected.

Nobel laureate Michael Levitt says the agreement between the clocks is what caught his attention, while stressing that the study cannot yet prove slower aging, since treating a lung condition could itself change the biomarkers.

The next test is Healthy volunteers. If those results hold, things get very interesting.

The first experiment is done. Now the race is to see whether AI can actually help us turn back the biological clock.

Source.

❗️OpenAI used $15 MILLION in tokens to tackle this 90-year-old mathematical mystery.

The Navier–Stokes equations describe how fluids move, from water swirling in a glass to air flowing over a wing. 

The mystery is whether a smooth 3D flow can remain stable forever, or tighten into a singularity where velocity becomes infinite in finite time.

OpenAI deployed 10,000 coordinating AI agents, which would cost an everyday user $15M in tokens, paired with a next-generation model. The system first solved a simpler version before producing a full result in just 88 hours.

The proposed solution identifies a vortex that spirals inward and stretches until the flow breaks down, while total energy remains finite.

The proof was then formally verified in Lean, allowing a computer to check every logical step.

The problem carries a $1 MILLION Clay Mathematics Institute prize, which OpenAI says it will not accept.
